headline: Two days of talks. One deal: a prisoner swap.
summary: Russia and Ukraine agreed Wednesday to a large exchange of prisoners of war, at their first meeting in nine months. Two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi produced no other breakthrough. The sides remain far apart on occupied land and on a role for Europe. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff fly to Moscow Thursday to see Putin.

cover_question.q: Why a swap but no ceasefire?

cover_answer: Both want their soldiers back. On land, they're far apart.
table_question: Do you have to trust someone before you trade with them?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Russia and Ukraine have been fighting a war for almost five years. This week their helpers sat at a table in a faraway city and agreed on one thing: soldiers each side is holding get to go home, maybe in a few weeks. Last year about 1,000 from each side went home, enough to fill 20 school buses. The grown-ups are working on the rest.
5-7.why: Soldiers going home is the one piece a six-year-old can hold. The war stays in one sentence.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the good piece: soldiers going home, counted in school buses. The war gets one plain sentence and no pictures. Expect 'why don't they just stop fighting?' The grown-ups at the table could not agree on that yet, and they meet again tomorrow.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Russia and Ukraine met for the first time in nine months, with the US in the middle. They disagree on the land Russia holds and on a seat for Europe. They agreed on one thing: a big swap of prisoners of war, maybe in three weeks. Like siblings who can't settle the room but hand back each other's stuff first.
8-12.why: Easy trade first, hard rules later: a chain they know from home.
8-12.why_long: At ten they are working out rules, so the script hands over the chain: nine months apart, two things nobody will move on, and one trade both sides want. The siblings are the mechanism: hand back the stuff before you settle the room. Expect 'who's winning?' Nobody at the table said. Both still want things the other says no to.

13-17.script: Why a swap but no ceasefire? Both want their soldiers home. On land, and on who sits at the table, they are nowhere. Kushner: "no trust right now", and a swap builds some. Second: Russia wants Europe out; Zelenskyy says no deal without it. Who gets a seat, the armies or everyone paying?
13-17.why: One real deal, a war no closer to ending. Which matters more?
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the swap is real and sends soldiers home, and the war is no closer to ending than in February. The script asks whether trust is built by small trades, and who belongs at a table where one side pays the other's bills. Expect 'is this just for show?' Zorin says three weeks. That is checkable.

5-7.a: In a war, each side holds soldiers it catches. Trading them back is how both sides get their people home.

8-12.a: A soldier caught by the other side and held until a trade or the end.

8-12.q: Why can't they agree to stop?
8-12.a: Russia wants to keep land it took. Ukraine says no. No trust yet.

13-17.q: Why a swap but no ceasefire?
13-17.a: Both want their soldiers home. On land, they're far apart.

13-17.q: Should Europe be in the room?
13-17.a: Zelenskyy says no deal without it. Moscow says Europe arms Ukraine.
